summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Mozambique. The colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision was struck from the penal code in the 2015 revision, and the code now in force, Law 24/2019 (effective 2020), carries no prohibition on consensual conduct or on gender identity. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of gender identity or consensual sexual conduct.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists in Mozambican law. Outright International's country entry, updated March 2026, records the continued absence of any mechanism for a person to change legal gender markers.

The penal code names gender identity in its hate-crime and hate-speech provisions. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on the basis of gender identity, and reaches defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 makes a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating factor in homicide. The Advertising Code (2016) bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation; that instrument does not name gender identity.

No legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in education, health, housing or employment. Employment non-discrimination protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships, and same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed locally as same-sex therefore has no recognised standing as a couple, and no relationship-based entitlement attaches.

Protection machinery exists and has a documented history. Lambda Mozambique, the country's only LGBT organisation, was blocked from NGO registration from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council, the highest court, ruled that the 'moral order' clause in Article 1 of Law No. 8/91 was unconstitutional, unblocking registration; a decade of earlier applications had been refused.

No dated incident of violence against a trans person in Mozambique appears in this record. What the sources document is discriminatory treatment: Lambda's Carina Capitine stated in June 2015 that the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests and contains no trans-specific material.

Societal attitudes are described by Outright International (updated March 2026) as broadly neutral, while LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education. Nothing in this record indicates whether these barriers are applied to foreign visitors.
tangentialFactors:
A regional public-opinion survey reported in March 2016 placed Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant countries: 56% of respondents said they would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, against 5% in Uganda, Burkina Faso and Niger. The measure concerns homosexual neighbours and does not speak to how trans people are treated.

Attitude data from 2017 is mixed. Support for same-sex marriage stood at 47% in Maputo, 38% in Beira and 42% in Nampula, and an ILGA poll that year found 61% of Mozambicans agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people, with 55% of respondents believing transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. The same 2017 survey found most respondents would not accept a child who came out, and 28% of Beira respondents said they would assault their child if gay; 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and would help if a person were being physically assaulted, and about one-third of respondents knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2013 survey found moderate support for parenting rights. All of these windows closed in 2013 or 2017.

An opposition party, PODEMOS, made a 2024 pledge on LGBT rights that raised expectations within the community before disappointing them, according to Outright International (updated March 2026).
localsOnly:
Residents who are LGBTIQ face family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education (Outright International, updated March 2026). The employment non-discrimination protection in force from 2007 was repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023 with effect from February 2024, so a resident worker dismissed on these grounds no longer has that statutory ground of challenge.

Lambda Mozambique operates as the country's only LGBT organisation, its registration secured only after the Constitutional Council's October 2017 ruling striking the 'moral order' clause. For residents, it is the principal point of contact for advocacy and documentation.

Organising predates the 2015 decriminalisation. The GlobalGayz archive records the first newspaper article arguing gay rights on 7 July 2006, petitions to parliament from men in Maputo, and an LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, all conducted under the colonial-era prohibition. Protests demanding same-sex marriage and common-law recognition have run since 2006.

A resident in a relationship classed locally as same-sex has no route to marriage or adoption, and no same-sex partnership carries legal recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources disagree on the instrument that removed the employment non-discrimination protection. One account attributes the repeal to Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024; another attributes it to a 2024 penal code change. Both agree the protection is gone as of 2024.

Not sourced: how Mozambican border, immigration or consular authorities treat a foreign identity document whose gender marker differs from the holder's presentation, whether such a document triggers secondary processing, and whether visa or arrival screening asks about gender identity. No source in this inventory addresses entry screening at all.

Not sourced: enforcement of the Article 191 and Article 160 protections. No case, prosecution or sentence applying either provision to a trans victim is documented here, and no source describes where trans prisoners are housed; the Human Rights Watch World Report 2024 chapter gives no trans-specific content on custody.

Not sourced: access to trans-related healthcare, hormones or competent clinical care, and treatment of gender nonconformity in policing practice. One summary source characterises hate crimes and violence against LGBTQ people as rare while discrimination occurs, but supplies no figure and no period for that characterisation, so it cannot carry a prevalence claim.
